question: Any links to Llyn Brianne (MU, archive, web) — deeper research

findings.mu: None of the 1,307 Mysterious Universe episodes mention Llyn Brianne, Rhandirmwyn, Cilycwm, Llandovery, Ystradffin, Tregaron or the upper Tywi (full-text and regex search of titles, show notes and link titles, 2026-10-30). Werewolf/dogman theme episodes exist (14.05 dogman reports, 27.01 Vargulfr, 30.12 Yoga Pants Lycanthropy, 33.23 Real Wolfmen) but none are Welsh.
findings.archive: Before this pass the private Llyn Brianne account had no links. It stays private (arc_links is readable by the anon key, so no link rows point at it); nearby public cases are grouped under the place entity upper-tywi-llyn-brianne instead.
findings.web_direct: No published UFO, ghost, cryptid or werewolf report names Llyn Brianne itself. Press coverage is about the dam, the drowned Fanog farm and the spillway kayaking ban.

place_history.fact: Named after the stream Nant y Bryniau; 'Brianne' was a mapmaker's misspelling that stuck.
Public inquiry Dec 1966; West Glamorgan Water Board (Llyn Brianne) Order 1968; opened by Princess Alexandra 15 May 1973. Protesters stopped a road through the Doethie valley.
Fanog (Fannog) farm drowned in 1973; its ruin/roof re-emerges in droughts (a joker once put a For Sale sign on it). Fanog Gorge photographed by Tom Lewis in the early 1900s.
Clay for the dam came from near Soar-y-Mynydd chapel; 91 m rock-fill dam, tallest in the UK; hydro station added 1996.
Dark Sky Discovery Site since October 2019.
Nantymwyn lead mine, Rhandirmwyn: possibly Roman, recorded 1304, 400+ workers at peak, closed 1932; several fatal accidents (inquests listed), no ghost lore found.
Twm Siôn Cati (c.1532–1609) married Joan, widow of Thomas Williams of Ystradffin, in 1607; cave on Dinas hill.

culture.fact: In White Wolf's Werewolf/Changeling 'Isle of the Mighty' setting, Llyn Brianne is one of three wandering sacred pools of Britain — fiction, but a werewolf-game connection to the name.

findings.nearest_wolf_like: Nearest wolf-like reports found are the Amman Valley 'wolfman' (c. 20 mi S, explained — a man living rough) and Tonmawr (c. 35 mi S). Everything else Welsh is North Wales or Meirionnydd.

new_cases.title: Wolfman of Merionethshire
new_cases.place: Meirionnydd, near a small station and disused slate quarries (exact place not given)
new_cases.desc: An amateur artist, Miss St Denis, staying at a farm, was followed from a small railway station by a silent figure; on a path among old slate quarries she saw it was human in form, covered in grey hair, with a wolf's head. It shrank from her torch and vanished. Locals said human and animal bones had been found in a nearby quarry and avoided the place after dark. Told in Elliott O'Donnell's Werewolves (1912) and later in Psychic News by John West. Pin is approximate (the farm is unnamed).

new_cases.title: Bipedal dog-like creature at Tonmawr
new_cases.place: Forest near Tonmawr, Neath Port Talbot
new_cases.desc: A witness who was 11 at the time (31 when he wrote in) was playing with cousins in the forest about a mile from a relative's home when he saw, some 20 ft away at the tree line, a dog-like animal standing on two legs, steadying itself on a tree with one paw before pushing off and standing in a threatening way. 'Werewolf isn't the word, this was, sure as day, a dog.' Anonymous, unverified account sent to Phantoms & Monsters (2024).

new_cases.title: Amman Valley 'wolfman' (explained)
new_cases.desc: Press called him the 'wolfman': a former forestry worker who lived wild in the woods from 2007, hunting rabbits and foraging, glimpsed by locals and leaving a stocked tin shack; food and milk went missing in a hard winter. Police appealed and searched with dogs in 2012 when he had not been seen for over a year. Not a creature: a man living rough. Included because it is the nearest 'wolfman' story to Llyn Brianne (about 20 mi south).

new_cases.title: Grey wolf-like animal, Craig-y-Don and Penrhyn Bay
new_cases.desc: A grey predator 'the size of an Alsatian, with a long snout' was reported around Craig-y-Don and Penrhyn Bay; a 70-year-old resident chased it off with stones at about 4am after it went for his cat. Cats went missing and the RSPCA interviewed owners. Suggested explanations: an escaped or released animal, or a misidentified large dog.

new_cases.title: Beast attacks carriage on the Denbigh–Wrexham road
new_cases.desc: A large beast attacked a two-horse carriage; one horse was mauled and the other broke free and bolted with the creature chasing it. A year later (1791) a farmer and blacksmith followed huge paw prints in snow to a farm where a dog had been killed; the farmer spoke of a beast with 'intelligent blue eyes'. Retold as Welsh werewolf lore; no original source is named, so treat as unconfirmed. Pin is the road's midpoint.

site_update.desc: Remote reservoir in the upper Tywi valley behind the tallest dam in the UK (91 m), opened by Princess Alexandra on 15 May 1973. The name is a mapmaker's slip for Nant y Bryniau. Fanog farm was drowned, and its ruin reappears in droughts. Clay for the dam came from near Soar-y-Mynydd chapel. Dark Sky Discovery Site since 2019. Twm Siôn Cati's cave, the Cilycwm witch and the wizard of Cwrtycadno are all within 7 miles. The spillway roars after heavy rain.

entity.name: Upper Tywi & Llyn Brianne
entity.summary: The upper Tywi valley around Llyn Brianne, Rhandirmwyn, Cilycwm, Ystradffin and the Doethie: the Cwrtycadno wizard, the Cilycwm witch, Twm Siôn Cati's cave, Strata Florida and the surrounding Cambrian Mountains cases (within about 12 miles of the dam).

dam_reports.name: Rhandirmwyn.net — Llyn Brianne
dam_reports.note: 1966 public inquiry, 1968 Order, protests that stopped a road up the Doethie, the Jones family of Troedrhiwruddwen losing land, Fanog farm drowned and re-emerging in droughts (someone once put a For Sale sign on it).

dam_reports.name: Cilycwm.com — Llyn Brianne, 'Little Switzerland'
dam_reports.note: Built for Swansea's heavy industry; work began Oct 1968, first water Oct 1972, opened 1973; spillway raised 1 m in 1995–96; hydro turbines and the buried power cable down the Tywi after a pylon fight.

dam_reports.name: Monmouthshire Beacon (2024) — 'The reservoir with a strange history'
dam_reports.note: The name mix-up, downstream fears the dam would burst, the legend of the engineer who slid the spillway on a shovel, extreme kayaking, dark-sky status.

dam_reports.name: BBC News (Nov 2008) — kayakers on the spillway
dam_reports.note: Kayakers riding the spillway in floods (used for about 20 years); Welsh Water called it dangerous and banned it. Bylaws in force from 2011 ban swimming and boating.

dam_reports.name: Wikipedia — Llyn Brianne
dam_reports.note: 91 m clay-core rock-fill dam (UK's tallest), clay dug near Soar-y-Mynydd, finished almost two years early, smolt trap for the Tywi salmon, 1996 hydro station.

dam_reports.name: Coflein — Fannog farmhouse (NPRN 3001)
dam_reports.note: The 19th-century farm drowned by the reservoir; probably the farm in Ruth Bidgood's 1969 poem 'At Fanog'. Pinned separately on the map.

dam_reports.name: People's Collection Wales — the Tywi before the dam (1966)
dam_reports.note: Peggy M. A. Jones's photo of farmland in the dry summer of 1966, from the 'Story of the forest' / Tywi Mountain archive at the National Library of Wales.

dam_reports.name: People's Collection Wales — Trawsnant (2010)
dam_reports.note: A pre-flooding farmhouse that survived, hidden a few hundred yards from the reservoir road.

dam_reports.name: Ecological Continuity Trust — Llyn Brianne Stream Observatory
dam_reports.note: Running since 1981 after acid rain was found in the streams: 14 catchments, liming in 1987–88, and cold-water insects down about 40% with warming.

new_sites: A 19th-century hill farm in the upper Tywi, drowned when Llyn Brianne filled in 1972–73. Its ruin and roof show again when the reservoir is low, and it was once reachable on foot. Probably the farm in Ruth Bidgood's 1969 poem 'At Fanog'. Grid ref SN 80880 51230 (Powys side of the reservoir).
